title: JavaScript
description: Learn to program with JavaScript, the language of the web: from your first line of output to classes and recursion; then map/filter/reduce, closures, errors and JSON, Map and Set, inheritance and, at university level, sorting and searching with complexity analysis, generators, reverse Polish notation, topological sorting of graphs, dynamic programming and backtracking.

js-01.title: Hello, world!
js-01.theory:
# Your first program

A program is a list of **instructions** that the computer runs one after another, from top to bottom. In JavaScript, the simplest instruction to show something on the screen is `console.log`:

```javascript
console.log("Olá, mundo!");
```

(`Olá, mundo!` is Portuguese for "Hello, world!"; the exercises in this track print their messages in Portuguese.)

The text between quotes is a **string** (a sequence of characters). You can use double quotes `"..."`, single quotes `'...'` or backticks `` `...` ``. Each call to `console.log` writes **one line** and moves on to the next.

```javascript
console.log("First line");
console.log("Second line");
```

## Why the semicolon?

The `;` marks the end of an instruction. JavaScript can usually guess where an instruction ends, but writing the `;` makes the code clearer and avoids surprises. We will always use it.

## Building text

With backticks you create a **template literal**: text that accepts values inside `${...}`. This will be very useful from now on:

```javascript
const nome = "Ana";
console.log(`Welcome, ${nome}!`);
```

(`nome` means "name"; we keep the variable names used in the exercise code.)

## Reading a line

In this track, programs receive data through **standard input**. The `prompt()` function (called **with no arguments**) returns the next line typed, as text. We will look at this carefully in lesson 3; for now, it's enough to know that:

```javascript
const nome = prompt();
console.log(`Hi, ${nome}!`);
```

## Common mistakes

- Forgetting to close the quotes or the parentheses: the program doesn't even start running (syntax error).
- Writing `Console.log` with a capital C: JavaScript is case-sensitive.
- Printing a message different from the one asked for: the grader compares the output **exactly**, letter by letter (spaces at the end of a line are ignored).
js-01.task:
Read a name (one line) and print exactly these three lines:

```
Olá, mundo!
Meu nome é <name>.
Estou aprendendo JavaScript!
```

(In English: "Hello, world!", "My name is <name>." and "I'm learning JavaScript!". The output must stay in Portuguese, exactly as shown.)

Example: for the input `Ana`, the output is:

```
Olá, mundo!
Meu nome é Ana.
Estou aprendendo JavaScript!
```
hints: Each line of the output is one call to console.log.
Use a template literal with backticks: `Meu nome é ${nome}.`
Check the period after the name and the accent on "é".

js-02.title: Variables and types
js-02.theory:
# Storing values

In lesson 1 you already used `const nome = prompt();`. This creates a **variable**: a name that points to a value stored in memory. In modern JavaScript there are two ways to create variables:

```javascript
const pi = 3.14;     // cannot be reassigned
let counter = 0;     // can change later
counter = counter + 1;
```

Prefer `const` and use `let` only when the value really needs to change. This keeps you from changing something by accident. (There is also the old `var`, which has confusing scope rules; avoid it.)

## Data types

Every value has a **type**. The main ones are:

- `string`: text, such as `"banana"`.
- `number`: numbers, whole or with decimal places (`42`, `-3.5`). JavaScript uses a single type for both.
- `boolean`: `true` or `false`.
- `null` and `undefined`: represent "no value".

The `typeof` operator tells you the type of a value:

```javascript
console.log(typeof "hi");   // string
console.log(typeof 42);     // number
console.log(typeof true);   // boolean
```

## Strings are also useful objects

Strings have **properties** and **methods**. `length` gives the number of characters; `toUpperCase()` and `toLowerCase()` return a new string in uppercase or lowercase; `at(-1)` gets the last character:

```javascript
const fruit = "banana";
console.log(fruit.length);        // 6
console.log(fruit.toUpperCase()); // BANANA
console.log(fruit.at(-1));        // a
console.log(fruit[0]);            // b
```

Note that the methods **do not change** the original string: strings in JavaScript are **immutable**. `fruit.toUpperCase()` creates a new text.

## Why do types matter?

The same operator does different things depending on the type. `+` adds numbers, but **concatenates** (joins) strings:

```javascript
console.log(2 + 3);     // 5
console.log("2" + "3"); // 23
```

This detail causes many bugs, which is why the next lesson explains how to convert text into a number.

## Common mistakes

- Trying to reassign a `const`: you get a `TypeError`.
- Writing `fruit.length()`: `length` is a property, with no parentheses.
- Thinking that `toUpperCase()` changes the variable: it returns a new string.
js-02.task:
Read a word (one line) and print four lines, exactly in this format:

Tamanho: <number of characters>
Maiúsculas: <word in uppercase>

```

(The labels are Portuguese for "Text", "Length", "Uppercase" and "Type"; keep them exactly as shown.)

Example: for the input `banana`:

```

Tamanho: 6
Maiúsculas: BANANA
Tipo: string
```

toUpperCase() returns a new string in uppercase.

js-03.title: Input and arithmetic
js-03.theory:
# Reading data and doing math

## How the input arrives

Each exercise is checked by an **automatic grader**. It runs your program several times and, in each run, **types by itself** the input lines of the test. You don't need to (and shouldn't) show messages like "Enter a number": the grader compares **all** of the output with the expected output, and any extra text makes the test fail.

To read, use `prompt()` **with no arguments**. Each call returns the **next line** of the input as a **string**, or `null` when the input has run out. `readline()` does the same thing.

```javascript
const a = prompt(); // first line
const b = prompt(); // second line
```

## The problem with text

Remember lesson 2? `+` concatenates strings. So:

```javascript
const a = prompt(); // "2"
const b = prompt(); // "3"
console.log(a + b); // 23  (!)
```

You need to **convert** the text into a number:

- `Number("42")` gives `42`; `Number("3.5")` gives `3.5`; `Number("abc")` gives `NaN` ("not a number").
- `parseInt("42", 10)` reads an integer in base 10, stopping at the first invalid character: `parseInt("42abc", 10)` gives `42`.
- `parseFloat("3.5")` reads a number with decimal places.

Use `Number` when the whole line must be a number; always pass base `10` to `parseInt`.

## Arithmetic operators

```javascript
console.log(7 + 2);  // 9
console.log(7 - 2);  // 5
console.log(7 * 2);  // 14
console.log(7 / 2);  // 3.5   (division keeps the decimal part)
console.log(7 % 2);  // 1     (remainder)
console.log(2 ** 3); // 8     (power)
```

For **integer division**, use `Math.trunc(a / b)`, which cuts off the decimal part toward zero. With negatives, `Math.trunc(-7 / 2)` gives `-3`, and the remainder `-7 % 2` gives `-1`: in JavaScript the remainder has the **sign of the dividend**. (`Math.floor` rounds down and would give `-4`; they are different things!)

## Decimal places

Numbers with a fractional part can come out with many decimal places (`0.1 + 0.2` gives `0.30000000000000004`, because of the binary representation). To show a value with a fixed number of decimal places, use `toFixed`:

```javascript
const average = 7 / 2;
console.log(average.toFixed(2)); // 3.50
```

`toFixed` returns a **string** with a dot as the decimal separator.

## Common mistakes

- Forgetting to convert and getting `"23"` instead of `5`.
- Using `Math.floor` when the task asks you to truncate.
- Printing "enter..." messages before reading.
js-03.task:

Resto: <a % b>

(The labels mean Sum, Difference, Product, Integer division, Remainder and Average; keep them exactly in Portuguese.)

Example: for `7` and `2`:

Math.trunc(a / b) does integer division, truncating toward zero.
For the average, use ((a + b) / 2).toFixed(2).

js-07.title: Arrays and strings
js-07.theory:
# Collections of values

An **array** stores several values in order, accessed by **index** starting at 0:

```javascript
const colors = ["blue", "green", "purple"];
console.log(colors[0]);      // blue
console.log(colors.length);  // 3
console.log(colors.at(-1));  // purple
colors.push("black");        // adds to the end
```

Unlike strings (lesson 2), arrays are **mutable**: `push`, `pop` and assignments like `colors[1] = "pink"` change the array itself. Even when it is declared with `const`, its contents can change; what `const` prevents is the variable pointing to another array (`colors = []` gives an error).

## Going through an array

```javascript
for (const color of colors) {
  console.log(color);
}
```

The `for...of` loop goes through each element. If you need the index, use the classic `for` from lesson 5.

## Methods that return something new

- `map(f)`: a new array with `f` applied to each item.
- `filter(f)`: a new array with only the items for which `f` gives `true`.
- `reverse()`: reverses **in place** (it changes the array!). To avoid changing it, copy it first: `[...arr].reverse()`.
- `join(sep)`: joins everything into a string.

```javascript
const nums = [1, 2, 3, 4];
const evens = nums.filter((n) => n % 2 === 0);
console.log(evens.join(", ")); // 2, 4
```

## From string to array and back

`split` breaks a string into an array; `join` does the opposite. This is the bridge between reading a line and working with its words (`palavras` means "words"):

```javascript
const sentence = "  the rat   ran ";
const palavras = sentence.trim().split(/\s+/);
```

`trim()` removes the spaces at both ends and `split(/\s+/)` splits on **one or more** spaces (a regular expression). Watch out: `"".split(/\s+/)` returns `[""]`, an array with **one** empty string, not an empty array! So handle the empty line separately, or filter: `.filter((p) => p !== "")`.

## Empty or missing line

If the input has no lines at all, `prompt()` returns `null`. The `??` operator provides a default value in that case: `const linha = prompt() ?? "";` (`linha` means "line").

## Common mistakes

- Printing the array with `console.log(arr)`: use `join` to control the format.
- Accessing `arr[arr.length]`, which is `undefined` (the last index is `length - 1`).
- Forgetting that `reverse()` changes the original array.
js-07.task:
Read a line with a sentence (the words may be separated by several spaces, and the line may be empty). Print:

```
Palavras: <number of words>
Invertida: <the words in reverse order, separated by one space>
Mais longa: <the longest word; in case of a tie, the one that appears first>
```

(Palavras = words, Invertida = reversed, Mais longa = longest; keep the labels in Portuguese.)

If there are no words, print only `Palavras: 0`.

Example: for `o rato roeu a roupa`:

```
Palavras: 5
Invertida: roupa a roeu rato o
Mais longa: roupa
```
hints: Use trim() and split(/\s+/), then filter out the empty strings.
To reverse without changing the original: [...palavras].reverse().join(" ").
When looking for the longest word, replace it only when the length is strictly greater (>), so the first one is kept in case of a tie.

js-08.title: Objects and classes
js-08.task:
Create a class `ContaBancaria` (BankAccount) with:

- `constructor(titular)` (`titular` = account holder): initial balance 0;
- `depositar(valor)` (deposit): adds to the balance;
- `sacar(valor)` (withdraw): if there is enough balance, subtracts and returns `true`; otherwise, changes nothing and returns `false`;
- a getter or method to check the balance (`saldo`).

Input: the account holder's name; then an integer `n`; then `n` lines, each one `D <amount>` (deposit) or `S <amount>` (withdrawal), with amounts that may have decimals.

For each operation print one line (amounts with 2 decimal places):

- `Depósito de <amount>` ("deposit of")
- `Saque de <amount>` ("withdrawal of") if it worked, or `Saldo insuficiente para sacar <amount>` ("insufficient balance to withdraw")

At the end: `Saldo de <account holder>: <balance>` ("balance of").

Example: for `Ana`, `3`, `D 100`, `S 30.5`, `S 200`:

```
Depósito de 100.00
Saque de 30.50
Saldo insuficiente para sacar 200.00
Saldo de Ana: 69.50
```
hints: Split each line with split(" ") and convert the amount with Number.
sacar must compare the amount with the balance before subtracting, and return true or false.
Use toFixed(2) on every amount you print.

js-09.title: Recursion
js-09.theory:
# Functions that call themselves

A **recursive** function solves a problem by calling itself on a **smaller** version of the same problem. Every recursion needs two parts:

- **Base case**: the simple situation, answered directly, that makes the recursion stop.
- **Recursive step**: shrinks the problem and trusts that the smaller call gives the right answer.

The classic example is the factorial: `n! = n * (n-1)!`, with `0! = 1` (`fatorial` is Portuguese for "factorial"):

```javascript
function fatorial(n) {
  if (n === 0) return 1;          // base case
  return n * fatorial(n - 1);     // recursive step
}
```

## What happens under the hood

Each call is kept on the **call stack**, waiting for the inner call to finish. `fatorial(3)` calls `fatorial(2)`, which calls `fatorial(1)`, which calls `fatorial(0)`. That one returns 1, and the answers come back multiplying: 1, 1, 2, 6.

If the base case is missing (or if the problem doesn't get smaller), the calls never stop and the program overflows the stack (in Node.js and in browsers you get `RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded`; in EasyCreator's built-in runner, the message "Recursão profunda demais", meaning "recursion too deep"). The stack has a limit of a few thousand calls, so recursion that goes too deep can fail even when it is correct; in those cases a loop is safer.

## Thinking recursively

The key question is: "if I already knew the answer to a slightly smaller problem, how would I get to the answer to this one?" For example, the sum of the digits of 1234 is the last digit (`1234 % 10 = 4`) plus the sum of the digits of `Math.trunc(1234 / 10) = 123` (`somaDigitos` means "sumDigits"):

```javascript
function somaDigitos(n) {
  if (n < 10) return n;
  return (n % 10) + somaDigitos(Math.trunc(n / 10));
}
```

Each call removes one digit, so the number of calls is the number of digits: the recursion takes about `log10(n)` steps.

## Precision limit

The `number` type only guarantees exact arithmetic with integers up to `Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER` (2^53 - 1, about 9 × 10^15). `18!` (about 6.4 × 10^15) is still below that limit; `19!` (about 1.2 × 10^17) is already above it, and from there on sums, divisions and remainders may come out rounded. For larger integers, JavaScript has `BigInt` (`20n`), which has no fixed size limit. In this exercise `n` goes up to 18, so `number` is enough.

## Recursion vs. loops

Anything you can do with recursion can be done with loops, and vice versa. Recursion shines on naturally recursive problems (trees, divide and conquer, like the merge sort in the next lesson); a loop usually uses less memory.

## Common mistakes

- A missing or wrong base case (for example, testing `n === 1` and calling it with 0).
- Forgetting the `return` on the recursive call.
- Using `/` without `Math.trunc`: decimals appear (1234 becomes 123.4, then 12.34…) and the sum comes out wrong, with decimal places instead of an integer.
js-09.task:
Write two **recursive** functions (no loops):

- `fatorial(n)` (factorial): returns `n!` (with `0! = 1`);
- `somaDigitos(n)` (sum of digits): returns the sum of the digits of an integer `n ≥ 0`.

Read an integer `n` (0 ≤ n ≤ 18) and print:

```
Fatorial: <n!>
Soma dos dígitos: <sum of the digits of n!>
```

(Fatorial = factorial, Soma dos dígitos = sum of the digits; keep the labels in Portuguese.)

Example: for `5`:

```
Fatorial: 120
Soma dos dígitos: 3
```
hints: fatorial: base case n === 0 returns 1; otherwise n * fatorial(n - 1).
somaDigitos: if n < 10 return n; otherwise (n % 10) + somaDigitos(Math.trunc(n / 10)).

js-10.title: Sorting and binary search
js-10.task:
Read an integer `n` (n ≥ 1), then `n` integers (one per line) and, finally, an integer `alvo` (the target).

1. Sort the numbers in increasing order by **implementing a sorting algorithm yourself** (insertion sort or merge sort; don't use `sort`).
2. Search for `alvo` in the sorted array with **binary search**.

Print:

```
Ordenado: <the sorted numbers separated by spaces>
Posição: <index (starting at 0) of the FIRST occurrence of the target in the sorted array>
```

or, on the second line, `Não encontrado` ("not found") if the target is not in the array.

(Ordenado = sorted, Posição = position; keep the labels in Portuguese.)

Example: for `5`, `8`, `3`, `5`, `1`, `3`, target `5`:

```
Ordenado: 1 3 3 5 8
Posição: 3
```
hints: Start with insertion sort: it's shorter. Test it with negative numbers.
In binary search, use the interval [ini, fim) and move ini to meio + 1 when v[meio] < alvo; otherwise fim = meio.
At the end, the target was found if ini < v.length and v[ini] === alvo.

js-11.title: Higher-order functions: map, filter and reduce
js-11.theory:
# Functions as values

In JavaScript, functions are values just like numbers and strings: you can store them in variables, put them in arrays and **pass them as arguments**. A function that receives or returns another function is a **higher-order function**. You have already used one without noticing: the comparator in `sort((x, y) => x - y)` from lesson 10.

## Arrow functions

The shortest way to write a function is the **arrow function**:

```javascript
const dobro = x => x * 2;               // one parameter: no parentheses
const soma = (a, b) => a + b;           // several: with parentheses
const media = (a, b) => {               // body with several lines: braces and return
  const s = a + b;
  return s / 2;
};
console.log(dobro(21), soma(2, 3), media(4, 7));   // 42 5 5.5
```

(`dobro` = double, `soma` = sum, `media` = average.) Without braces, the value of the expression is returned automatically.

## map: transform each element

`arr.map(f)` creates a **new** array with `f` applied to each element. The original doesn't change.

```javascript
const precos = [10, 25, 8];
const comDesconto = precos.map(p => p * 0.9);       // [9, 22.5, 7.2]
const etiquetas = precos.map((p, i) => `${i + 1}: R$ ${p}`);
```

(`precos` = prices, `comDesconto` = with discount, `etiquetas` = labels.) The function also receives the **index** as a second argument, if you want it.

## filter: pick elements

`arr.filter(f)` keeps only the elements for which `f` returns true:

```javascript
const caros = precos.filter(p => p >= 10);   // [10, 25]
```

## reduce: accumulate a result

`arr.reduce(f, initial)` walks through the array carrying an **accumulator**. For each element, `f(accumulator, element)` returns the new accumulator:

```javascript
const total = precos.reduce((acc, p) => acc + p, 0);          // 43
const maior = precos.reduce((m, p) => (p > m ? p : m), -Infinity);
```

The accumulator can be anything, even an object. A classic use is **grouping**:

```javascript
const vendas = [
  { cat: "fruta", valor: 5 },
  { cat: "pão", valor: 3 },
  { cat: "fruta", valor: 2 },
];
const porCat = vendas.reduce((acc, v) => {
  acc[v.cat] = (acc[v.cat] ?? 0) + v.valor;
  return acc;
}, {});
// { fruta: 7, pão: 3 }
```

(`vendas` = sales, `valor` = amount, `porCat` = by category.) Always pass the **initial** value: without it, `reduce` uses the first element and breaks (TypeError) on an empty array.

## Chaining

Since `map` and `filter` return arrays, you can chain the operations into a **pipeline** that reads from top to bottom:

```javascript
const totalCaros = vendas
  .filter(v => v.valor >= 3)
  .map(v => v.valor)
  .reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0);
```

Other methods in the same style: `find` (the first one that matches), `some` (any?), `every` (all?), `forEach` (just walks through, returns nothing) and `Object.entries(obj)`, which turns an object into an array of `[key, value]` pairs, great for sorting or mapping afterwards.

## Why does this matter?

A `for` loop mixes **how** to walk through the data with **what** to do. With `map`/`filter`/`reduce`, you state only the intent, and each step is small and easy to test. This is the style of **functional programming**, widely used in JavaScript (React, Node) and in data processing.

## Common mistakes

- Forgetting the `return` in an arrow function with braces: it returns `undefined`.
- Forgetting to return the accumulator in `reduce`.
- Using `map` just to walk through, without using the new array: use `forEach`.
- To return an object directly from an arrow, wrap it in parentheses: `x => ({ valor: x })`.
js-11.task:
Read an integer `n` and then `n` lines in the format `<product> <category> <quantity> <price>` (names without spaces; quantity and price are integers; all products are different). A product's revenue is quantity × price. Print:

```
Faturamento: <sum of the revenue of all products>
Por categoria:
- <category>: <revenue of the category>
Mais vendido: <product> (<quantity> unidades)
Preço >= 10: <products with price greater than or equal to 10, separated by ", ">
```

(Faturamento = revenue, Por categoria = by category, Mais vendido = best seller, unidades = units, Preço = price; keep the labels in Portuguese.)

The categories appear in alphabetical order (ordinary string comparison). The best seller is the one with the largest quantity (on a tie, the one that came first). The expensive products appear in input order; if there are none, print `Preço >= 10: nenhum` ("none"). There will always be at least one product.

Use `map`, `filter` and `reduce` instead of loops for the calculations.

Example: for the input

```
4
suco bebidas 3 7
pao padaria 10 1
cafe bebidas 2 15
bolo padaria 1 30
```

the output is:

```
Faturamento: 91
Por categoria:
- bebidas: 51
- padaria: 40
Mais vendido: pao (10 unidades)
Preço >= 10: cafe, bolo
```
hints: Revenue: `itens.map(it => it.qtd * it.preco).reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0)`.
To group, use `reduce` with an object `{}` as the initial value and add into `acc[it.categoria]` (with `?? 0` the first time). Then sort `Object.keys(...)` with `sort()`.
The best seller: `reduce((m, it) => (it.qtd > m.qtd ? it : m))` (with a strict `>`, the first one wins the tie). The expensive ones: `filter` by price and `map` to the name.

js-12.title: Scope and closures
js-12.task:
Write:

- `criarOperacao(op, k)` (create operation), which returns a function of a number `x`: for `soma` (sum), `x + k`; `mult`, `x * k`; `pot` (power), `x ** k`; `resto` (remainder), `x % k` (JavaScript's `%`, with the sign of `x`);
- `compor(fns)` (compose), which returns a function that applies the functions in `fns` in sequence (with an empty list, it returns the value itself);
- `contarChamadas(f)` (count calls), which returns an object `{ chamar, total }`: `chamar(x)` ("call") calls `f(x)` and counts the call; `total()` tells how many calls there were. The counter must stay **private**, in a closure.

Read an integer `n` and `n` lines `<op> <k>` (integers). Then read an integer `m` and `m` integer values, one per line. Build the composition of the `n` operations, in order, wrap it with `contarChamadas` and, for each value `x`, print `f(<x>) = <result>`. At the end, print `Chamadas: <total()>`.

(Chamadas = calls; keep the label in Portuguese.)

Example: for the input

```
2
soma 3
mult 2
3
1
10
-3
```

the output is:

```
f(1) = 8
f(10) = 26
f(-3) = 0
Chamadas: 3
```
hints: `criarOperacao` returns different arrow functions depending on `op`, each one using the captured `k`: for example `if (op === "soma") return x => x + k;`.

js-14.title: Map and Set: counting and comparing
js-14.theory:
# Keyed collections: Map and Set

Arrays are great for sequences, but terrible for questions like "has this word appeared yet?" or "how many times?": searching an array is **O(n)** (lesson 10). For that there are two structures based on **hash tables**, which answer in **O(1)** time on average.

## Set: a collection without duplicates

A `Set` stores **unique** values. Adding a value that is already there does nothing.

```javascript
const s = new Set();
s.add("azul");
s.add("verde");
s.add("azul");             // ignored
console.log(s.size);       // 2
console.log(s.has("verde"));   // true
s.delete("verde");
```

The most famous trick: removing duplicates from an array in one line.

```javascript
const unicos = [...new Set([3, 1, 3, 2, 1])];   // [ 3, 1, 2 ]
```

The `...` (*spread*) "spreads" the values of anything iterable into an array. A `Set` keeps the **insertion order**.

## Set operations

With `filter` and `has`, the operations from math become straightforward:

```javascript
const a = new Set([1, 2, 3, 4]);
const b = new Set([3, 4, 5]);
const intersecao = [...a].filter(x => b.has(x));    // [ 3, 4 ]
const diferenca = [...a].filter(x => !b.has(x));    // [ 1, 2 ]
const uniao = new Set([...a, ...b]);                // {1, 2, 3, 4, 5}
```

(`intersecao` = intersection, `diferenca` = difference, `uniao` = union.) Each `has` is O(1), so the intersection costs O(|a|), instead of O(|a|·|b|) with arrays.

## Map: a real dictionary

A `Map` associates **keys** with **values**:

```javascript
const idades = new Map();
idades.set("Ana", 15);
idades.set("Bruno", 17);
console.log(idades.get("Ana"));      // 15
console.log(idades.get("Zé"));       // undefined
console.log(idades.has("Bruno"));    // true
console.log(idades.size);            // 2
```

(`idades` = ages.) Why not use a plain object `{}`? A `Map`:

- accepts **any** type of key (numbers, objects), and doesn't convert everything to a string;
- has no hidden "inherited" keys (a plain object already "has" `toString`, `constructor`...);
- knows its size with `size` and keeps insertion order;
- is made for frequent insertions and removals.

## The counter pattern

Counting occurrences is probably the most common use of a `Map`:

```javascript
const contagem = new Map();
for (const p of palavras) {
  contagem.set(p, (contagem.get(p) ?? 0) + 1);
}
```

(`contagem` = count, `palavras` = words.) To walk through it: `for (const [chave, valor] of contagem)`. To sort, turn it into an array of pairs with `[...contagem]` and use `sort` with a comparator that breaks ties:

```javascript
const ranking = [...contagem].sort((x, y) => y[1] - x[1] || (x[0] < y[0] ? -1 : 1));
```

Read it like this: compare by count (descending); if it gives 0 (a tie), the `||` moves on to the alphabetical comparison. The `[key, value]` pairs can be destructured right in the parameters: `([p, c]) => ...`.

## Cleaning up text

To count words properly, normalize first: `toLowerCase()` makes everything lowercase, and a regular expression strips punctuation from the ends:

```javascript
const limpa = p => p.toLowerCase().replace(/^[.,!?;:]+|[.,!?;:]+$/g, "");
```

`^` is the start and `$` the end of the text; `[.,!?;:]+` means "one or more of these characters"; the `g` replaces every occurrence.

## Common mistakes

- Using `map[chave] = valor` on a `Map`: this creates an ordinary property, and `get` doesn't see it. Use `set` and `get`.
- Expecting `new Set([[1, 2], [1, 2]])` to have size 1: different arrays are different objects, even with the same contents.
- Forgetting to break ties when sorting: the output then depends on the input order.

js-17.title: Stacks and reverse Polish notation
js-17.theory:
# Expressions without parentheses

We write `3 + 4 * 2` with the operator **between** the operands: this is **infix** notation. It's comfortable for humans, but it requires precedence rules and parentheses. In 1920, the Polish logician Jan Łukasiewicz proposed putting the operator **before** the operands; the variant with the operator **after**, **reverse Polish notation** (RPN, or postfix), became famous in HP calculators and is still used today inside compilers and virtual machines.

- `3 + 4` becomes `3 4 +`
- `3 + 4 * 2` becomes `3 4 2 * +`
- `(3 + 4) * 2` becomes `3 4 + 2 *`

Notice: in RPN **there are no parentheses** and no precedence rules. The order of the tokens already says everything.

## A stack

The central structure of this lesson is the **stack** (LIFO: last in, first out). In JavaScript, an array with `push` and `pop` is a stack, with both operations in O(1); the top is `p[p.length - 1]` (or `p.at(-1)`).

## Evaluating RPN

Evaluating RPN with a stack is surprisingly simple:

- number: push it;
- operator: pop **two** values (`b` comes out first, then `a`), compute `a op b` and push the result.

At the end, the stack must have **exactly one** value: the answer. If an operand is missing when an operator comes, or more than one value is left at the end, the expression was invalid.

```
3 4 2 * +
stack: [3] -> [3, 4] -> [3, 4, 2] -> [3, 8] -> [11]
```

Careful with the order: in `10 2 -`, the result is `10 - 2`, not `2 - 10`.

## Converting: the shunting-yard algorithm

Edsger Dijkstra (the same one from the shortest-path algorithm) created the **shunting-yard** (named after a railway yard where trains are sorted) to convert infix into RPN, with an **operator stack** and an **output queue**. Go through the tokens:

1. **Number**: goes straight to the output.
2. **Operator** `o1`: while the top of the stack is an operator `o2` that must be applied **first**, move `o2` to the output. "First" means: `o2` has **higher** precedence, or **equal** precedence and `o1` is left-associative. Then push `o1`.
3. **`(`**: push it.
4. **`)`**: move operators from the stack to the output until you find the `(`, which is discarded. If the stack runs out without finding `(`, the parentheses are unbalanced.
5. At the end, move the rest of the stack to the output. If a `(` shows up there, a parenthesis was never closed.

Precedences: `^` (power) = 3, `*` and `/` = 2, `+` and `-` = 1.

## Associativity

`8 - 3 - 2` is `(8 - 3) - 2 = 3`: subtraction is **left**-associative. Power, on the other hand, is **right**-associative: `2 ^ 3 ^ 2` is `2 ^ (3 ^ 2) = 2 ^ 9 = 512`, not `(2 ^ 3) ^ 2 = 64`. That's why, in step 2, a `^` doesn't pop another `^` off the stack: the second one is applied **first**.

Full example: `3 + 4 * 2 / (1 - 5) ^ 2 ^ 3` becomes `3 4 2 * 1 5 - 2 3 ^ ^ / +`.

## Cost

Each token enters and leaves the stack at most once: the conversion and the evaluation are **O(n)**. The same scheme (convert to a linear form and then run it with a stack) is what the JVM, Python's virtual machine and WebAssembly do: they are all **stack machines**.

## Tokenizing

First of all, break the text into tokens: numbers with several digits become a single token, operators and parentheses are one-character tokens, spaces are ignored. A practical test for digits is `c >= "0" && c <= "9"`.

## Common mistakes

- Swapping `a` and `b` when popping (gets subtraction, division and power wrong).
- Treating `^` as left-associative.
- Forgetting to check for a leftover `(` at the end of the conversion.

In the shunting-yard, when you see an operator `t`, pop to the output while the top is an operator and (`PREC[topo] > PREC[t]` or (`PREC[topo] === PREC[t]` and `t` is not `^`)). On a `)`, pop until the `(`; if the stack empties first, the parentheses are unbalanced.

js-18.title: Graphs: dependencies and topological sorting
js-18.theory:
# Dependency graphs

A **graph** is a set of **vertices** connected by **edges**. When the edges have a direction, the graph is **directed**: `A → B` doesn't imply `B → A`. A very common kind of directed graph is the **dependency** graph:

- Courses and prerequisites: Calculus 1 → Calculus 2.
- Tasks in a project: foundation → walls → roof.
- Software packages: `npm` has to install the dependencies before whatever depends on them.
- Spreadsheets: a cell can only be computed after the ones it uses.

## Representation

For each vertex, store the list of vertices its edges point to (**adjacency list**), and also how many edges **arrive** at it (its **in-degree**):

```javascript
const adj = new Map();       // vertex -> array of neighbors
const grauEntrada = new Map();
for (const v of vertices) {
  adj.set(v, []);
  grauEntrada.set(v, 0);
}
// edge a -> b
adj.get(a).push(b);
grauEntrada.set(b, grauEntrada.get(b) + 1);
```

(`grauEntrada` = in-degree.)

## Topological sorting

A **topological sort** is an order of the vertices in which every edge `A → B` has `A` before `B`: a valid order in which to take the courses. It exists **if and only if** the graph has no **cycle** (it's a *DAG*, a directed acyclic graph). If `A` depends on `B` and `B` depends on `A`, no order works.

## Kahn's algorithm

The idea is the same as someone putting together a class schedule: start with what has no prerequisite.

1. Put all the vertices with in-degree 0 in a list of **available** ones.
2. While there are available ones: take one out, `u`, and add it to the order. For each edge `u → v`, "erase" the edge by decreasing `v`'s in-degree; if it reaches 0, `v` becomes available.
3. If the order ended up with every vertex, great. If any were **left over**, there is a cycle: those vertices never reached in-degree 0 (they are in a cycle or depend, directly or indirectly, on something that is).

Each vertex goes in and out once and each edge is erased once: **O(V + E)**.

There are usually **several** valid orders. To get a single answer, a common rule is to always pick the **alphabetically smallest** available one. With an array, that means sorting or searching for the smallest at each step, O(V) per choice; with a **priority queue** (heap), O(log V).

## Longest path in a DAG

What is the minimum number of semesters needed if there's no limit on courses per semester? A course can only be taken in the semester after the one of its **last** prerequisite:

```
semestre[v] = 1 + max(semestre[u]) for each edge u -> v   (or 1, if there are none)
```

(`semestre` = semester.) Processing the vertices in **topological order**, all of `v`'s prerequisites already have their semester computed when we reach it. The answer is the largest semester, which is the number of vertices on the graph's **longest path** (the "critical path" of project management). This is dynamic programming over a DAG, and it costs O(V + E).

Watch out: in an **arbitrary** graph, finding the longest path is an extremely hard problem (NP-hard). The absence of cycles is what makes it easy here.

## DFS: the other way

A topological sort also comes out of a **depth-first search**: the **reverse** of the order in which the vertices finish being explored is topological. DFS detects cycles when it finds an edge to a vertex that is still "in progress" in the recursion.

## Common mistakes

- Reversing the direction of the edge (`A B` means `A` comes **before** `B`).
- Forgetting to check whether the order has every vertex: without that, a cycle goes unnoticed.
- Counting the in-degree twice for repeated edges and decrementing only once.

js-20.title: Backtracking: the N queens problem
js-20.theory:
# Searching methodically

Some problems ask you to find **all** the configurations that obey certain rules: filling in a sudoku, generating passwords, scheduling shifts, solving a maze. Generating every possibility and then filtering is usually unfeasible: their number grows absurdly fast. **Backtracking** is the organized way to do this search, **cutting off** dead ends as early as possible.

## The N queens problem

Place `N` queens on an `N × N` board so that **no queen attacks another**. The chess queen attacks along the same row, the same column and both diagonals. For `N = 8` (the chessboard), there are 92 solutions; the problem was studied by Gauss in the 19th century.

Naive brute force: choosing 8 squares out of 64 gives more than **4 billion** combinations. But we can be smart:

1. Two queens never share a row. So place **exactly one per row**, from top to bottom. The problem becomes "choose a column for each row".
2. When placing a queen, check right away whether it is attacked by the previous ones. If it is, **don't even continue** down that path.

## The backtracking scheme

```javascript
function resolver(linha) {
  if (linha === n) {
    // all rows filled: we found a solution
    return;
  }
  for (let c = 0; c < n; c++) {
    if (pode(linha, c)) {
      colocar(linha, c);       // choose
      resolver(linha + 1);     // explore
      tirar(linha, c);         // undo (the "backtrack")
    }
  }
}
```

(`resolver` = solve, `linha` = row, `pode` = can, `colocar` = place, `tirar` = remove.) It's always the same rhythm: **choose, explore, undo**. The recursion (lesson 9) draws a **decision tree**: each level is a row, each branch a column. When a test fails, that whole branch is **pruned**: none of the millions of configurations below it are visited.

## Checking attacks in O(1)

Testing all the previous queens costs O(N) per attempt. You can do it in O(1) with three sets of marks:

- `coluna[c]`: is there already a queen in column `c`?
- On the diagonal that goes down to the right, `row − column` is **constant**. Use `diag1[linha - c + n - 1]` (the `+ n - 1` avoids a negative index).
- On the diagonal that goes down to the left, `row + column` is constant: `diag2[linha + c]`.

```javascript
const pode = (l, c) => !coluna[c] && !diag1[l - c + n - 1] && !diag2[l + c];
```

`colocar` marks all three as `true`; `tirar` unmarks them. This swap of "check everything" for "keep an up-to-date summary" is a very common trick in algorithms.

## Search order and the first solution

Since the columns are tried in increasing order, row by row, the solutions are found in **lexicographic order** (like words in a dictionary, comparing the column of row 1, then that of row 2...). The first one found is the lexicographically smallest. For `N = 4`, the columns (counting from 1) are `2 4 1 3`.

## Complexity

Backtracking is still **exponential** in the worst case: the number of N queens solutions grows roughly like `N!` divided by an exponential. Pruning doesn't change the complexity class, but it reduces the nodes visited by many orders of magnitude: for `N = 8`, the search visits only about 2 thousand partial boards (some 15 thousand squares tested), instead of billions.

Many "hard" problems (sudoku, graph coloring, the traveling salesman) are tackled this way. They belong to the **NP-complete** class: nobody knows a polynomial algorithm for them, and finding out whether one exists is the **P = NP** question, one of the great open problems in mathematics.

## Common mistakes

- Forgetting to **undo** the choice after the recursive call: the marks "leak" into the other branches.
- Storing the solution found by reference to an array that keeps being modified: copy it (`[...pos]`) at the moment you find it.
- Getting the diagonal offset wrong and accessing a negative index.
